title: Give release.yml's registry verification a longer window with backoff, distinguishing 'not yet visible' from 'wrong content'
description: Counterpart of quest-cli's QCLI-247. The registry-propagation lag on @opum-ai/lore-linux-arm64 specifically has now recurred on three consecutive releases and is strictly worsening, not random jitter: 0.4.5 resolved in ~15s, 0.4.6 in ~35s, 0.5.0 took ~25 minutes (resolved 2026-09-08T14:49:18Z) before registry.npmjs.org's versions map showed the just-published 0.5.0 -- confirmed via response headers directly (cf-cache-status/age) that this was a genuine origin-side gap, not a stale CDN cache. npm's own publish confirmation (the job log's '+ @opum-ai/lore-linux-arm64@0.5.0' line) was correct every time; only the registry read API lagged. This release, the lag ran long enough that opum-cli-e2e independently flagged it as a possible install-breaking defect before it resolved on its own -- a false alarm that cost real investigation time on both sides. See docs/reference/lore-cli-release-truth.md's 0.5.0 entry for the full timeline and evidence.

acceptanceCriteria.text: release.yml's post-publish registry verification step polls with a longer window and backoff (not a fixed short timeout), sized against the observed 3-release lag history (up to ~25+ minutes) rather than the historical ~35s worst case

The verification step's failure output distinguishes a version genuinely missing from the registry ("not yet visible", retry/backoff territory) from a version present but reporting different content/metadata ("wrong content", a real defect worth escalating immediately) -- these must never be reported identically
The three-release lag history (0.4.5 ~15s, 0.4.6 ~35s, 0.5.0 ~25min) is recorded as the evidence justifying the new window, so a future session does not re-diagnose this from scratch

finalSummary:
Delivered in BOTH the workflow the criteria name and the script the release actually runs. The criteria named release.yml only; 0.6.2 publishes manually via scripts/publish-release.sh because OIDC is dead (LCLI-482), so satisfying them literally would have ticked all three boxes and left the real release exposed to the exact false alarm this task exists to prevent. Widened deliberately, with the orchestrator's explicit agreement.

TWO THINGS THE TASK ASSUMED THAT WERE NOT SO. release.yml had NO post-publish verification at all -- the publish job was six steps and ended on the publish loop -- so this was 'build one', not 'lengthen one'. And publish-release.sh had three unguarded npm view calls, the worst being the final npx smoke, which on failure called die with 'the packages are published but the install path is broken. Investigate before announcing.' With the known 25-minute lag that fires a scary, wrong message seconds after the one irreversible step of a release.

WHAT SHIPPED, both files:
  - One SHARED wall-clock window, not one per package. The deadline starts once and every still-missing package is re-polled against it, so the total wait is bounded at 30 minutes however many of the seven are outstanding, and each still gets the whole remaining window. Per-package would either be too short for the slowest or serialise seven waits into hours. Both files say which, in the code, so a maintainer hitting a paused release can tell immediately that it is ONE window.
  - Window sized from evidence, not taste: 30 minutes because the worst observed was 25 and the trend is upward (0.4.5 ~15s, 0.4.6 ~35s, 0.5.0 ~25min). Backoff doubles 5s to a 60s cap, so polls land at 5, 15, 35, 75, 135s -- the first three bracket the two smaller observed lags, then it settles into minute intervals for the tail.
  - The two failures are separated. NOT VISIBLE YET is propagation, is not a defect, and never fails the run. VISIBLE WITH WRONG BYTES is real and fails immediately. release.yml proves the second by comparing the registry's dist.shasum against the sha1 of the tarball THAT JOB published -- a version-string check would pass against a registry serving the right version with the wrong tarball, which is the failure nobody would catch by eye.
  - The exhaustion message is the most valuable line here and is written to be unmissable: it states that npm already confirmed the publish, that this is NOT proof of failure, and that npm unpublish is the wrong tool and destructive. The window it guards against is 72 hours wide and would be reached for by someone who has just been told their fresh release is broken while it is in fact fine.

VERIFIED BY EXECUTION, not inspection. The script helper was extracted from the real file and driven against stubs for three cases: all-visible (returns 0 immediately), becomes-visible on the third poll (returns 0 at 15s), and never-visible (respects the deadline exactly, emits the warning, returns 1). The workflow step was extracted from the parsed YAML and run against three REAL tarballs with a stubbed registry: all-match exits 0; one package never propagating exits 0 with a ::warning:: and does not fail; one package serving different bytes exits 1 with a ::error:: and still checks the remaining packages first rather than stopping at the first mismatch.

PORTABILITY, which forced a design change worth recording: the script runs on macOS, whose /bin/bash is 3.2, where expanding an EMPTY array under set -u aborts -- so the pending set is a space-separated string, not an array. The workflow step originally used declare -A, which needs bash 4+; the runner has it but no maintainer could run the step locally to test it. Removed it and re-derived name/version per tarball instead, because code in a release path that cannot be run locally cannot be tested locally. shellcheck -S style is clean on both apart from one pre-existing SC2012 at line 83 that predates this change.
